stories.summary_ja:
**主な議論点**  
記事「『I just chose words carefully』」では、語彙選択の慎重さがテーマとなり、特にタイポをそのまま残すべきか修正すべきか、フォントやレイアウトへのこだわり（例：ウィドウ/オーファン禁止）が話題になった。さらに、LLMを使って同様の言葉選びを自動化する試みにも関心が集まった。

**賛否両論**  
タイポを意図的に残すことに対しては、「原文の雰囲気を保つ」という賛意と、「誤りは読者に混乱を与えるので直すべき」という反対意見が分かれた。また、ウィドウ/オーファンを避けるレイアウト制約については、文章のリズムを整える有益な手法だという支持と、過度な制約が創造性を害するという批判があった。

**注目コメント**  
ウィドウとオーファンの定義を挙げて説明したコメントは、レイアウトへのこだわりがどのように執筆スタイルに影響するかを具体的に示しており、多くの読者に「気づき」を与えたと評価された。また、LLMを用いて同じ言葉選びを自動化する動画を紹介したコメントは、技術と伝統的な文筆の融合点として注目された。
stories.editor_note: 言葉選びが単なる言語の問題ではなく、エンジニアのコミュニケーションやAIプロンプト品質に直結する点が注目されています。日本の開発現場でも、誤解を招かない仕様書作成やコードコメントの重要性が再評価されています。

comments.author: semiquaver
comments.text: > because apparently what we have to offer is worth spending a ton of cycles to calculate the Anubis challenge. This statement holds the core misapprehension behind Anubis. It’s not a ton of cycles. There is no difficulty setting that would be inconvenient for bots but usable for humans on mobile devices. I noticed the other day that lists.ffmpeg.org had moved to Anubis difficulty level 6, which takes ~180sec for my iPhone 17 to solve at ~100KH/s, making the site unusable. So I spent ~10 minutes vibe coding a safari extension with a native bridge to an optimized C kernel using ARM SHA256H* instructions that can do 200+ MH/s on the same device. This solves Anubis difficulty level 6 in a handful of milliseconds. Given the numbers and capabilities involved (a single $5K ASIC miner yields 200TH/s, a million times more hash rate than my optimized kernel running on an iPhone), I don’t see how proof of work could possibly be a sustainable strategy to keep bots out without ruining human user experience. It’s an arms race that can’t be won. Edit: I encourage you to try this yourself. Here's a sample prompt that ought to one-shot the task: > Build an iOS Safari Web Extension that accelerates Anubis proof-of-work using a native C ARM64 SHA-256 kernel. Precompute the invariant 128-byte challenge prefix, search fixed-width decimal nonces with ARM SHA-2 intrinsics and two worker threads, and target difficulty-6 solves under one second. Relay challenges from a Safari content script through the background service worker to native code, then submit the valid nonce/hash through Anubis’s normal pass-challenge endpoint. Include a deterministic benchmark app, correctness tests against CryptoKit, bounded execution, and fallback to Anubis’s stock solver.

comments.author: robotmay
comments.text: I've spent the last few days adding traps to one of my websites, ironically using LLMs of course, and I've been having quite a lot of fun doing it. Instead of the proof-of-work system of Anubis, I've gone down the iocaine route but implemented it in my application itself, as it's built in Elixir and causing problems for scrapers is really fun when it takes almost no server resources. Currently I trick bad scrapers into a fake infinite black hole path with the promise of tasty data, then serve images to them one byte at a time over 15 minutes (after sending the header quickly), bloat the responses to cost them tokens, and randomly return AI generated images of sexy toasters. I have an admin dashboard with a little leaderboard for which ones get the most stuffed, and it keeps my heart warm on these wet autumn evenings.

comments.author: justAnotherHero
comments.text: While nowhere near compared to their scale, I run a consumer app where most of our users are using the mobile app, with the web app getting perhaps 10-15% of the mobile active users. However day after day it just gets blasted with requests for deep pages. I was quite alarmed when I saw a 100x increase in the daily active user numbers which relied on session length, only to realize they were all bots. Naively I too initially resorted to blocking user agents(Meta is thankfully nice enough to identify themselves, not nice enough to stop blasting 50k requests a day however), IP ranges from cloud providers and various browser fingerprints that I found connected to suspicious traffic. However the battle seems unwinnable at the moment, outside of gating all content behind auth which I don't want to do. We have around 500k user generated content pages and I want those to remain publicly available. I would be happy to provide our data to any one of these scrapers and I even added a message asking them to contact us if they want access to our data whenever I return a 403 response, however nobody has reached out. Another campaign that someone is constantly running is daily checks for 100s of possible secret/config paths in hopes of finding an exposed private variable, these i've just blocked even though they would return a 404. I still haven't found a way to deal with rotating residential IPs however, and most likely never will. My current approach is to just run a 24 hour scan of all requests with codex and update my next.js proxy with more IP ranges, browser fingerprints and anything else that won't affect a real person. Has anyone managed to come up with a way to stop this onslaught of crawlers and scrapers?

comments.author: mzajc
comments.text: > Why is git.kernel.org “interesting” to crawlers I think the post underestimates just how little thought and effort is put into these bots. I also run a cgit instance with far less interesting projects, and am not spared from the deluge of HTTP requests. The explanation I could come up with is that they try to crawl all links regardless of how much sense it makes or how much load it causes. cgit being cgit, this means billions of links for all combinations of parameters and hashes. That, or it's a deliberate DDoS attack.

comments.author: sgsjchs
comments.text: Ironically, defense by obscurity may be the way to go here. Fork Anubis. Slightly modify the hash function it computes. Deploy. Do not try to make your fork widely adopted. Do not even publish it. You've just defeated ASICs and any craweler that's special-cased Anubis (currently all of them). If enough people do this, the only recourse they will have is either genuinely executing served js code like a real user or building some unholy pipeline that uses ai agents to compile it to a GPU kernel for every host.

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、Anubisのような proof‑of‑work（PoW）ベースのボット対策が実際には人間ユーザーの体験を損なうほど重く、一方で最適化されたネイティブコードやASICで簡単に突破できるため「勝てない武装競争」だという指摘だった。これに対して、PoWを使わずに偽の無限パスやバイト単位の遅延レスポンス、AI生成画像を返す「iocaine」方式や、IP・UA・フィンガープリントのブロック、さらにはAnubisをフォークしてハッシュ関数を変更し obscurity で防御する案が挙げられた。賛否は、PoWの持続不可能性に同意する声と、人間に負荷をかけずにボットだけを困らせる仕掛けを楽しむ声に分かれた。特に注目されたコメントは、iPhoneでARM SHA‑256 intrinsicsを使ったSafari拡張を自作し、Anubis難易度6をミリ秒で解くことができたという実証で、PoWが bot 対策として機能しないことを示した点だった。また、フォークして非公開にすればASICや特化ボットを無力化できるというアイデアも注目された。

stories.summary_ja: 教皇レオ14世の『Magnifica Humanitas』に関する議論では、AIの進路は技術そのものに決まらず、人間の選択とそれを支える制度、そして共通善に資するよう革新を管理する責任にかかっているという指摘が中心となった。賛成側は、この言葉が倫理的・社会的視点を欠くシリコンバレーの巨額投資よりも示唆に富むとし、教会の社会教義が現代技術論に貢献できると評価した。反対側は、カトリック教会が長年にわたる金権主義、性的虐待の隠蔽、中絶避妊への反対などで利益追求と権力の濫濫を繰り返してきた歴史を挙げ、教皇の説教は説得力に欠けると批判し、宗教機関の発言に懐疑的であることを示した。特に注目されたコメントとして、「アメリカの億万長者よりも教皇の方がAIについて実践的なことを言える」という驚きと、AIの方向は選択と制度次第だという具体的な指摘が挙げられた。
stories.editor_note: 教皇レオ14世の文書は実在せず、風刺やAI生成コンテンツの見分け方が議論の焦点となっています。日本でもディープフェイクや偽情報への警戒が強まり、メディアリテラシー教育が急務となっています。

comments.author: SyneRyder
comments.text: Just a heads-up for those trying it out, I've found a couple of regressions in Beta 6 that rendered my Haiku system unbootable, until I remembered about hammering the space key during the boot sequence to get to the safe mode menu. In my case, my ThinkPad X1 (Yoga 3rd Gen) used to boot despite what appeared to be kernel panics, but typing "continue" at the kernel prompt would skip past them and everything would then work fine. In Beta 6, it now hangs at boot instead with no kernel panic warning. Disabling ACPI in the safe mode options gets me past that, and there's a way to disable ACPI permanently at boot via some configuration files - though obviously that isn't desirable. It also seems there's been some work on USB Audio (yay!), but it now causes a kernel panic on boot if a Focusrite Scarlett is connected. Turning the Scarlett off avoids the kernel panic. The Scarlett has never officially worked in Haiku, but it at least never used to crash the system. In my case, I've reverted back to the USB Audio Scarlett Haiku driver that Claude Sonnet vibe coded for me, and for me that's working. (I can't contribute that code because of Haiku rules against AI code, but hopefully the humans will eventually find time to hand code it and get it working.)

comments.author: TacticalCoder
comments.text: Funny to see that frontpage as earlier on today I made a comment saying that with LLMs I'm betting we'll see N-modular redundancy systems soon, with a ultra-hardened, minimal, part picking the majority votes of N LLM-written implementations (in different languages, on different stacks, all running at the same time). Not 100% TFA but "computing in space" involved a lot of N-modular redundancy systems. The reason I'm 99.9% sure we'll see that is that it'll help catch both bugs in the LLMs implementations themselves (and we know there are plenty of those) but also in the stacks/platforms/VMs running those software. Imagine one spec and five implementations (Rust, Go, Java, Python, whatever) and one minimal system, with the tiniest of the tiniest attack surface, returning the answer as soon as 3-of-5 agree. And, as a bonus, if later on one the two "missing" answer arrives and doesn't match, it's cause for enquiry and bugs be smashed. Basically (and although I don't care about Ethereum or cryptocurrencies except for the cryptographic aspect), we already witnessed that: 3 different implementations of Ethereum and, in the early days, one of the implementation whose result differed from the two others. And hence the implementation not respecting the spec (in that case it was the only one that was faulty) got instantly detected (and promptly patched). My memory is fuzzy but I know this happened. Heck, I may write a proof-of-concept for fun. I've got other ideas as to what will be possible in the future but I'm keeping them for another day.

comments.author: adrianwaj
comments.text: "The card never actually transmits a message back to your phone. Instead, it changes how much energy it absorbs from the field, and your phone detects those power dips and converts them to binary data. Most NFC tags use this harvested energy only to run their internal circuitry, but some NFC chips are able to take excess DC voltage and route it out to external hardware. This business card uses that last feature." I wonder if it can be applied to robo-couriers and drone drop-offs. One of those comes to your door, you get your stuff, and you pass something that is powered-up over its sensor and it drives off. It's the equivalent of signing-off on a delivery. The sensor obtains and stores information about you as well. Maybe I've got it wrong and the recipient needs the sensor and the driver has the powered device that only switches on when it is ready to do the drop off. With this card, what are the information transfer and storage scenarios? Would be great to see a table. Can the two parties both exchange and store information with minimal power? A card with a little battery and power-on button? Card can have some type of port? Can it be be used as a crypto wallet with a kill switch in the event of a robbery or home invasion? I think this is important in Hub-and-Spoke communities (previous comment) where population densities decrease but there'll still have to be a lot of exchange going on. Offline-based interactions are a good idea too - keep the airwaves clean.

stories.summary_ja:
主な議論点は、NFCフィールドからエネルギーを収穫し吸収量を変調してデータを送り、余剰電圧で外部ハードウェアに給電できる点と、これを使った配達確認・ドローン受領・暗号ウォレットなどの応用アイデア、さらに既存NFCデバイスの干渉や給電量の不足への懸念、カードの見た目やLEDカスタマイズへの関心である。  
賛否両論：賛成側は革新的で極低消費電力、デザインの美しさ、LEDの色・位置・サイズ・明るさを自由に設定できる点、将来的にpiezoブザーで音を鳴らせる可能性を評価した。否定側は財布内の多数NFCタグによる混線リスク、harvestedエネルギーだけでは双方向通信やキルスイッチ付きウォレットは実現困難で、バッテリやポート追加が必要だと指摘した。  
注目コメント：ドローンやロボ配達時の受領サインとして利用でき、ハブ・アンド・スポーク地域でのオフライン情報交換に適するという洞察、piezoブザーでモデムダイヤルアップ音を再現できるという具体的アイデア、そして5〜10枚パックで安価に注文しカスタムLEDを自由に配置したいという要望が特に目立った。
stories.editor_note: NFCエナジーハーベスティングとMCUを組み合わせた名刺は、バッテリー不要のIoTタグとして実用性が評価されています。日本の交通系ICカードやSuica連携サービスへの応用可能性が指摘され、スタートアップの製品開発ヒントとなっています。

comments.text: > [in 2020/2021] the dominance of autoregression was not as well-established as it is today: GPT-3 had turned some heads, but the ‘ChatGPT moment’ wouldn’t come until late 2022 I disagree with this. Decoders were absolutely dominant in 2020 for chat. GPT2 was considered too dangerous to release, and I remember scrambling to get on the GPT3 waitlist. It worked. (The only exception I will make is encoder-decoder models which now are often done by decoder-only.) But what made it go mainstream was RL. RLHF at first, then other improvements like DPO that were less of a pain in the ass to set up. Adding diffusion on top of that would be an even bigger pain in the ass. Before ChatGPT there really wasn’t much of a concept of pre-training and post-training. It was all pre-training. Post training was what made the bots conversational and not just “continuing the thing you wrote to them”. So in short, diffusion never took off because it was just a more complicated way to generate tokens, and the real problem was getting tokens in the right distribution.

comments.author: bborud
comments.text: An architect friend of mine once said that he admired IKEA above all other furniture manufacturers because it made a modern range of aesthetics available to the masses. IKEA had done more to evolve the public taste than any other manufacturer. And I do have to agree. I can remember what ghastly furniture most shops used to have around here. There was a lot of what we call "cabin furniture" - which isn't made to look good, just be practical. (Well, some people like that look, but it is a bit...dull). Sure, there was more solid wood furniture, but guess what: that durability comes at a cost. Not only in terms of money, but also in terms of how easy it was to install and move. And who buys furniture to pass it on to your kids? Your kids will be unburdening themselves of your old furniture before you are in the ground. As for quality: I have owned some pricey designer furniture and I can't say that I'm always impressed with the quality. Yes, if you have a lot more money you can get really well built furniture. But IKEA is more often than not more than sufficient quality. (Also see their "hidden tags" campaign) If I pay $5000 for a chair I have reason to expect a lot from it. And more often than not, pricey furniture doesn't actually deliver sufficient quality to be able to defend the price. (Collectible furniture is a whole different deal where you don't actually care all that much about quality, but more about it being an original piece). For those of you who look down on IKEA furniture, I'd like to hear about what alternatives you think need mentioning. Especially for young people or people of modest means. And I'm not trying to make some clever rhetorical point here. I can't really think of any company that offers what they offer and comparable quality, looks and price here in Europe.

comments.author: amluto
comments.text: This seems weak. In a language like Rust, the compiler will “lock” the pointers for you, and you can’t forget. In a language like C++ (and presumably Zig), one could, in theory at least, have the iterators and slices that reference the storage of a dynamic array hold some sort of lock that pins the storage. But this API requires the programmer to remember to lock the pointers and also requires the programmer to keep the lock alive for the correct region of code. And it looks to me like even the example in the blog post has the lock taken completely outside the function that requires stability, so there is nothing whatsoever that gets the lock scoping right. Even the type system can’t help — the offending parse function can’t declare that it wants a pointer-locked ArrayList parameter.

comments.text: Aside: one Zig (syntax) feature that I really missed in Rust is shown in the second code block, namely prefixed multi-line string literals à la: const text = \\This is a long comment \\But I can split it among lines arbitrarily \\And keep my indentation. ; I've started using the Rust macro library `docstr` [1], which does the same thing: const TEXT: &'static str = docstr!( /// Now I can do it in Rust, too. /// I prefer this style a lot of the time /// for long texts. ); It even works with macros (example from the docs): let greeting: String = docstr!(format! /// Hello, my name is {name}. /// I am {} years old! age ); 1. https://docs.rs/docstr/latest/docstr/

stories.summary_ja:
**主な議論点**  
Zig の ArrayList に新たに導入された「ポインタ安定性（pointer stability）」機能について議論が交わされている。具体的には、可変長配列の要素へのポインタが再確保によって無効化されないよう、プログラマが手動で `lock`／`unlock` を行う API が提案されている点が焦点となっている。

**賛否両論**  
賛成側は、C++ の `vector` イテレータ無効化や Rust の所有権チェックに比べて、Zig がこの問題を言語レベルで扱う姿勢を評価し、「ファーストクラスの懸念事項」として歓迎している。一方、批判側はロックの付け忘れやスコープ管理がプログラマに負担となり、型システムで強制できない点が弱いと指摘し、代わりにインデックスや未リンクリストなど別のデータ構造を使うべきだと主張している。さらに、ロックが関数の外側で取られている例が示され、スコープの安全性が保証されないことを懸念する声もあった。

**注目コメント**  
- 「C++ 開発者は常に `vector` イテレータの無効化に悩まされている。Zig がこれを第一級の懸念として扱うのは歓迎すべき進歩」というコメントは、機能への肯定的評価を代表するものとして挙げられた。  
- 別のコメントでは、Zig のマルチライン文字列リテラル構文（`\\` でプレフィックス付き）が Rust にはなく便利だと指摘し、Rust の `docstr` マクロで代替していることを紹介していた。  

このように、ポインタ安定性の実装方法とその使い勝手が議論の中心であり、言語設計のトレードオフと代替アプローチについて多角的な意見が交わされた。

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、QubesOSの非常に小さい攻撃対象領域にもかかわらず、Dom0からのcopy-to-VM操作時にエラー報告バックチャネルを悪用して特権昇格が可能になるという脆弱性の深刻さと、その影響範囲がDom0を日常作業に使わない利用者に限定される点だ。賛否については、設計が堅牢だからこそ驚きだと指摘する意見と、Dom0を使わなければリスクは実質的に小さいとみなす意見が分かれた。注目されたコメントとして、エラー報告バックチャネルという見落とされやすい攻撃ベクターを指摘し、これがQubesOSほどのセキュリティ志向システムでも見つかることを示した意見や、グラフィックハードウェアアクセラレーションの欠如が普及の妨げになっているという指摘があった。

stories.summary_ja:
**主な議論点**  
雨から電気を取り出す仕組みが実用的かどうかが中心に議論された。特に大規模発電への適用は困難であり、湿潤環境での小型電子機器への補助電源としての可能性が指摘された。また、雨が金属を腐食させる「電気雨」現象が石材でも起こるか、酸性雨（プロトン化雨）との関連も疑問視された。

**賛否両論**  
賛成側は、洞窟や熱帯雨林、シャワーなど日照が得られにくい場所でのニッチな用途に期待し、低コストでメンテナンスフリーな電源として有用だと主張した。反対側は、電気雨による金属腐食が設備寿命を縮め、大規模導入ではメンテナンスコストがかさむため実現性が低いと指摘し、酸性雨による化学反応と混同されやすい点も懸念材料とした。

**注目コメント**  
「巨大な金属ドームに水をかければ十分な負の静電気が蓄積し、スパークギャップで放電できるのではないか？」というアイデアが提案され、これを科学展示のネタにできるかもしれないという洞察が得られた。また、「石材でも同様の現象が起こるか」という疑問が投げかけられ、材料依存性についてさらに実証実験が必要だという指摘があった。
stories.editor_note: 電気雨が金属を腐食させる現象は、大気中の汚染物質と湿度が組み合わさった結果であり、インフラの耐久性に直結します。日本の梅雨シーズンや沿岸部では塩害と酸性雨の複合影響が懸念されており、防食塗料や材料選定の指標となっています。

stories.summary_ja:

・賛否両論: 一方、ボイラープレートの増加は保守性の低下やバグの混入リスクを懸念する声が多く、特に大規模アプリケーションでの長期サポートに不安がある。他方で、関数型言語の宣言型・不変データの利点を活かしつつ、GTK4の豊富なウィジェット群やCSSスタイルシート機能を直接利用できる実現可能性を評価する意見もあり、抽象化レイヤーやコード生成ツールの導入が解決策として挙げられている。  
・注目コメント: 「GTK4に関数型言語でバインディングしようとする苦労はよくわかる。確かに検証が難しく、特殊ケースばかりのCボイラープレートが大量に発生する」という指摘は、実装における実際の痛みを端的に表しており、今後はメタプログラミングや自動バインディングジェネレータを活用してボイラープレートを削減し、型安全性を確保する方向性が求められていることを示唆している。
stories.editor_note: Lambdockは、Dockの代替として機能拡張とカスタマイズ性を追求したオープンソースプロジェクトです。日本ではmacOSユーザーの間で、ワークフローに合わせたダックカスタマイズのニーズが高まっており、こうしたコミュニティ駆動のツールが注目されています。

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、Reddit で提示された「地球上で最長の水上直線ルート」が本当に最長かどうかを検証し、アルゴリズムと標高データで確認したこと、および同様に陸上最長ルートを求めた論文の内容である。コメントでは、海路は確かに最長だと認めつつ、陸路については海抜以下を水とみなすルールが問題だと指摘され、サヘル付近から中国へ至るより長い陸路が見落とされているという議論が中心となった。賛否は、海路の結果についてはほぼ全員が賛同したが、陸路については標高フィルタリングの妥当性を巡って意見が分かれ、一部は死海付近を避けるべきだと主張し、他は論文の方法が妥当だと擁護した。注目コメントとして、GCMAP のリンクを提示し実際のルートを可視化したユーザーの指摘や、サヘルから中国へのルートを死海除外で考えるとさらに長くなるという詳細な解説があり、これが議論の焦点となった。
stories.editor_note: 地球上で最長の直線経路（陸路または水路）を示した研究は、地理学的好奇心と測量技術の進歩を象徴しています。日本列島の形状を考慮すると、国内での同様の経路探索は観光ルート設計や災害避難路の検討に応用できます。

comments.author: mike_hearn
comments.text: Linux isn't like macOS, it doesn't have any kind of proper desktop sandboxing architecture that really works. So this is kind of security theatre. If you run a malicious program it can do stuff like tamper with your PATH or exploit local vulns in apps to get to the point where it can control anything that matters (which root generally doesn't). For instance it can just drop a custom shell into ~/.bin/.hidden-shell and reconfigure the terminal emulator to run it. So this kind of "vulnerability" doesn't seem that important. If you run code as yourself on Linux it owns you. On macOS it's very different. Pervasive code signing gives all apps a stable identity enforced by the kernel that they can't easily escape. The kernel can then impose sandboxing policies on any app that's run regardless of how it's installed, for instance, preventing apps from rummaging through ~/Documents or monitoring your screen. Permissions are editable and guaranteed to stick, including across upgrades. And root is disempowered so obtaining it barely matters, it's only really there for UNIX compatibility. Unfortunately implementing an Apple style architecture on Linux would be very difficult.

comments.text: I’m baffled by the idea that the agents might have edited their own transcripts. Sure, a copy of Claude Code or Codex or Pi can edit its transcripts. But AFAICT this whole thing was part of an RL workload, and surely the RL system itself has a separate record of all the inputs and rollouts along with an indication of which model checkpoint produced them so that it can feed back into the training code. I find it hard to believe that OpenAI would skip this part and try to train on the transcripts stored by the (inherently untrustworthy) agent harnesses instead, if for no other reason than that the logits generated as part of the rollouts are useful and it’s not free to recalculate them. (I believe that some modern RL systems explicitly account for the minor numerical logit differences between the inference engine and the training engine.) Conversely, if OpenAI is blindly feeding transcripts from inside their agent sandboxes into their training engine, then I think they're being unbelievably irresponsible and that they should assume that their "cyber" agents have compromised themselves by editing those transcripts.

I’ve long been encouraging my European friends to not take the abundance of growth for granted, and now we see it in the environment, plain and clear: the worlds’ weather is changing. A week of sweltering heat is predicted for us again in Vienna, and as we get started on September and then October so close, two thoughts are on my mind: use this opportunity to go for more dips in the Danube, and .. Sunlight never reaches the ground because of the tall giant trees so there's no undergrowth. It's just dead leaves and mushrooms. comments.text: I'm not completely convinced by this comparison between blind chess and prompting LLMs. In blind chess you get deterministic information about the state of the board: each mental update to your board model can be precise, and you have the full state at every point in time. LLMs are notoriously non-deterministic, and even at temperature zero you still can't predict exactly where the weights will take you next. I suppose you can get closer to deterministic if you adopt a prompting style where you almost dictate every line of code, but at that point the coding agent is more of a typing assistant. The productivity benefits of coding agents unlock themselves when you figure out how to turn short prompts - "add tests that exercise the registration form and check the happy path and all failure states" - into larger changes. If you're completely blind to the results of those you're going to end up with a system you don't 100% understand very quickly. In blind chess terms you'll no longer know the positions of every piece on the board.

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、ブラインドチェスとLLMへのプロンプト作業の類比が適切かどうかである。コメントでは、ブラインドチェスは盤面の状態が決定的で常に把握できるのに対し、LLMは温度0でも非決定的であり、完全にコントロールできない点が指摘され、その結果として「タイピングアシスタント」になるリスクがあると論じられた。一方で、プロンプトを通じて高レベルの概念を組み立てる「思考の時間」が創造性や問題解決に重要だと擁護する意見もあり、専門家がAIを活用するほど効果が高まるという実証例も紹介された。類比は抽象的な教訓としては有用だが、決定論と非決定論の違いを深追いすると破綻するという指摘もあり、意見は分かれた。注目すべきコメントとして、ブラインドチェスでの正確な状態把握とLLMの予測不能さを対比し、短いプロンプトで大きな変更を試みると理解不能なコードが生まれやすいという洞察が挙げられた。また、アナロジーは「領域ではない」というメタ認知的注意喚起も見られた。
stories.editor_note: 父が90年代に教えてくれたAIコーディングの話は、当時のルールベースシステムや初期の機械学習実装を思い出させ、技術の歴史的継承を感じさせます。日本の第一次AIブームでは、専門機や論理プログラミングが盛んでした；今日のディープラーニングブームへの教訓として、過去の失敗と成功を振り返る動きが研究者間で広がっています。
